title: The Sea and the Throne: Daniel 7-8, Job 21, John 13, Jude 1-7
summary: Daniel 7-8 opened the visions half of the book: chapter 7 dated to Belshazzar's first year (about 553 B.C., when Nabonidus left for Tayma), so before chapter 5; the Aramaic section (2:4 to 7:28) framed by two four-kingdom visions, the statue as a king sees empires and the beasts as heaven sees them. The beasts were taught as Babylon (the lion made to stand like a man, read by Hippolytus as Nebuchadnezzar of chapter 4, paraphrased), Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome; the throne scene set the horn's 'great words' against the court and the opened books. On 7:13, bar enash ('a human being'), a Ligonier devotional was quoted (singular, not Israel; 'only God uses the clouds as a chariot'), and the hard question, second coming or ascension, was answered with Calvin (paraphrased: ascension, 'came to the Ancient of Days') against Henry and Hippolytus (last judgment); the one NT move was Mark 14:62. Chapter 8 (Hebrew again, Susa, Ulai) covered the ram and goat named by Gabriel, Alexander's death in 323 B.C., and the little horn as Antiochus IV Epiphanes ('Epimanes', per JFB citing Polybius), the Zeus altar in 167 B.C. and cleansing three years later, with the 2,300 evenings and mornings mentioned as days or sacrifices; the second hard question, whether the horns of 7 and 8 are the same, was answered no, with Porphyry's late-date view stated and Jerome quoted against it (Judas Maccabaeus did not come with the clouds), Calvin (Caesars) and Jerome and Hippolytus (Antichrist) paraphrased, Antiochus as a preview of the pattern, and Hippolytus quoted ('not to anticipate the counsel of God, but exercise patience and prayer'). Daniel 8:27 closed with Spurgeon No. 2788 (1878) quoted ('his visions did not make him visionary'); the application was that prophecy is given to steady you, not to make charts: look at the throne, then go about the King's business. Job 21:1-21 was taught as Job's direct answer to Zophar 20:5 and Bildad 18:5 (Barnes on 21:17), with Gregory's Moralia 15 quoted ('not by their words but by their ways, Depart from us') and Henry paraphrased (this is not the world of retribution); practical point: don't read hearts from bank accounts, don't call God unjust because the reckoning is later. John 13:12-17 covered Teacher and Lord, the argument from greater to less, whether foot washing is a sacrament (Sproul paraphrased: no, its cleansing belongs to baptism; Calvin paraphrased: no annual ceremony but lifelong readiness; Augustine paraphrased: literal washing can awaken humility), and Chrysostom Homily 71 quoted twice (schoolmasters' beautiful letters; 'to know belongs to all; but to do, not to all'). Jude was introduced (half-brother of Jesus via James, Mark 6:3; Clement of Alexandria paraphrased on 'servant' not 'brother'; 60s A.D.; close to 2 Peter 2), with v3 'once for all delivered' (Henry paraphrased), v4 grace turned into permission, the three examples, the 'Jesus' reading in v5, and Calvin quoted on v5 ('torpid in a cold knowledge'). The closing connection was knowing and doing: Job's wicked refusing knowledge, Jude's readers who once knew, 'if you know these things', and Daniel who did not understand yet rose to work.
threads: Daniel 9 is next: Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12, 29:10) in the first year of Darius the Mede, his great confession prayer (9:4-19, 'we have sinned', 'for your own sake'), Gabriel's arrival 'at the time of the evening sacrifice' (9:21), and the seventy weeks (9:24-27), with the anointed one cut off and the abomination. Spurgeon No. 2788 'Prayer for the Church' (Daniel 9:17, June 20, 1878, via preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_daniel) is fetched and mostly unused: 'the prayer that lies in the soul, like eggs in a nest', 'Daniel's prayer was the child of thought', 'They seem to be so taken up with the future that they do nothing in the present', 'the very best way to wait for the coming of the Master is to be found doing his will'. Precept Austin also lists Spurgeon on Daniel 9:26 and the sermon 'Shutting, Sealing, and Covering, or Messiah's Glorious Work' (9:24). Jerome's commentary (tertullian.org jerome_daniel_02_text) has a long survey of the seventy weeks views (Africanus, Eusebius, Hippolytus, Clement, Origen, Tertullian). Calvin on Daniel 9 at biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/daniel/9.htm.

Unused Daniel 7-8 material: Henry 'The empires of the world were beasts that rose out of the sea; but Christ's kingdom is from above: he is the Lord from heaven' and 'he will not cut them off at once, but wear them out by long oppressions' (7:25) and 'As long as we live in this world we must have something to do in it' (8:27); Calvin quoting 'The greatest kingdoms are the greatest robberies' (7:2) and his explanation of 'like' a son of man (Christ not yet incarnate; Irenaeus's 'prelude', Tertullian's 'specimen of humanity'); Hippolytus on 7:13 'who makes the days old, and yet becomes not old Himself'; Jerome 'none of the prophets has so clearly spoken concerning Christ as has this prophet Daniel'; JFB on 8:27 'He who holds nearest communion with heaven can best discharge the duties of common life'; Barnes on 8:27 secular duty; Ligonier 'One like a Son of Man' 'commentators are by no means united on the meaning of each image'; Keil arguing 2,300 evening-mornings cannot mean 1,150 days; time, times and half a time (7:25) not discussed.

Job 21:22-34 is next: 'Will any teach God knowledge?' (21:22), one dies in full vigor and another in bitterness, yet 'they lie down alike in the dust' (21:26), the testimony of travelers (21:29), the wicked 'spared in the day of calamity' (21:30), and 'How then will you comfort me with empty nothings?' (21:34), closing the second cycle; Eliphaz opens the third cycle in chapter 22. Spurgeon No. 410 is on Job 21:29-31. Gregory Moralia Book 15 (lectionarycentral.com/GregoryMoralia/Book15.html) continues through 21:24, with Book 16 after. Unused Job 21:1-21: Gregory 'it is one thing not to have known, and another thing not to have chosen to know', 'prosperity in the present life is no witness to innocency', 'except the patience of God bore with them, they would never live long in their sins'; Henry 'Justly will God say Depart... to those who have bidden him depart' and 'no certain judgment can be made of men's character by their outward condition'; Keil linking 21:7 to Asaph's near-ruin in Psalm 73.

John 13:18-30 is next: 'I know whom I have chosen', Psalm 41:9 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me' (a warranted OT quotation), 'I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that... you may believe that I am he' (13:19), Jesus troubled in spirit, the beloved disciple reclining at his side, the morsel given to Judas, 'Satan entered into him', and 'And it was night' (13:30). Chrysostom Homily 71 already covers 13:18 ('O what forbearance! Not yet does He convict the traitor'); Augustine Tractates 59-62; Calvin at biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/13.htm (13:18-20 follows the part used). Unused 13:12-17: Augustine Tractate 58 'when the body is bent at a brother's feet' (paraphrased only); Calvin 'until a man has learned to yield to his brethren, he does not know if Christ be the Master'; Chrysostom 'He who sits upon the Cherubim washed the feet of the traitor'; Ligonier 'The Example of Jesus' (2018) 'if a task such as foot washing was not beneath Him, neither should we consider any form of service beneath us'.

Jude 8-16 is next: the intruders 'relying on their dreams', Michael disputing with the devil about the body of Moses ('The Lord rebuke you', v9; the Assumption of Moses tradition), the way of Cain, Balaam's error, Korah's rebellion (v11), the five pictures from nature (hidden reefs at love feasts, waterless clouds, fruitless trees twice dead, wild waves, wandering stars, vv12-13), and Enoch's prophecy (vv14-15, quoting 1 Enoch 1:9; handle the canon question in a sentence). Clement of Alexandria's Adumbrations (newadvent 0211) cover these verses ('Clouds... who do not possess in themselves the divine and fruitful word'; 'Twice dead'); Calvin continues at biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jude/1.htm; Henry mhcw. Unused Jude 1-7: Calvin on v3, 'as though he had blown a trumpet to awake them from their torpor', and on v4, 'nothing is more pestilential than men of this kind, who from the grace of Christ take a cloak to indulge in lasciviousness'; Henry 'not the discriminating badges of this or the other party'; Ellicott on v5 'Jesus' reading; the 'kept' wordplay (v1, v6, then v21 and v24) set up but not fully developed; v6 angels (original fall vs Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch) not discussed.

Voices quoted this episode: Ligonier Ministries ('One like a Son of Man', 2013), Jerome (Commentary on Daniel 7), Hippolytus (Scholia on Daniel 7:7), C. H. Spurgeon (No. 2788, 1878), Gregory the Great (Moralia 15 on Job 21:14), John Chrysostom (Homily 71 on John, twice), John Calvin (Jude 5). Paraphrased: Matthew Henry (Daniel 7 intro, Job 21, Jude 3), Hippolytus on 7:4, Calvin on Daniel 7:13 and the Caesars and John 13:15, JFB on Epimanes, Barnes on Job 21:17, R. C. Sproul ('The Foot Washing'), Augustine Tractate 58, Clement of Alexandria (Adumbrations on Jude). Desiring God still returns 403; no Piper today.

show_notes: Daniel's visions begin: four beasts from the sea, the Ancient of Days, and one like a son of man coming to the throne, then the ram, the goat, and the little horn of Antiochus Epiphanes. Also Job's question about why the wicked prosper, Jesus explaining the foot washing, and the opening of Jude, with Jerome, Hippolytus, Spurgeon, Gregory the Great, Chrysostom, and Calvin.
